name: Marco Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. This is confidential. Tell me what an ordinary day at the contact centre is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27 and lead a call and chat team at a contact centre. A two-year college diploma got me in, but handling hard complaints is what made me lead. I earn the usual rate for this job and have about four months of expenses saved. I live with my partner, Rosa, and we have no children.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy finding the real cause of a failed order while everyone else is reading the same script. I use an AI note tool every day, though I check each summary before it leaves my screen. We visit Rosa’s parents on Sundays, and I try not to carry a customer’s anger into that meal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau is much like our current note helper: a speed boost, not a new boss. I’d still check the summary before promising a customer anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is safe enough, but I dislike spending my savings when Rosa and I talk about a future home. Four months of savings is a cushion, not permission to stop paying attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the team in 2026 and use the note tool on routine calls. In the first year of small change, I’d put the time saved into coaching new agents and add a fixed amount from each pay to our home fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm at work and a little watchful about our plans. The centre still needs somebody who can hear when an order story does not add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a new agent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d show Niko, the new agent on my shift, how to compare a draft summary with the actual order record. Last week the draft missed a second delivery, and that would have sent the customer back around the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the saved money go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa (my partner) and I keep the home fund separate from day-to-day money. I would add to it after payday, even if the amount is small.

say: I’d call AI a **note helper** that still needs a person to check it.
I’d tell new agents to compare summaries with **order records**.
think: I believe my **job is safe** while small AI changes leave our normal call work in place.
I still want to protect our **home fund**.
do: Keep **leading calls** and using checked AI notes in 2026.
Coach new agents and add a **fixed amount** to the home fund in the first year.
feel: **Calm** about work, watchful about household plans.
S0.quote: Four months of savings is a cushion, not permission to stop paying attention.
fieldNote: He trusts **checked AI notes** because he uses them daily.
His **home fund** motivates saving even without a job threat.
He teaches agents to compare a draft with the **actual order record**.

steps.text: Keep leading calls and checking AI notes against order records
Add a fixed amount from each pay to the home fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will take the easy chats first, and the centre should put strong agents on exceptions. I’d tell the team to learn the new tool while the company is still paying us to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can stay useful if I can find errors and coach people, but fewer hires may eventually mean fewer leads. Some other centres are within reach, yet they may be buying the same software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask to test the automated reply queue and record the mistakes it makes. In the first year routine chats move, I’d apply for a paid exception-review post and offer to train new agents on cases that need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened. I like trying a tool, but the headcount makes me watchful. The payroll office counts seats, not pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you prove a review role is useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would track failed refund answers for a month, then show my manager the cases and the time I saved correcting them. If that turns into a paid review post, I’d take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start another source of income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my uncle to let me help with two weekend appliance repairs, as a trial. I learned from him before, and an extra small income would help if call hours thin out.

say: I’d tell colleagues **easy chats** will move first.
I’d urge the team to learn the **paid tool** while we can.
think: I think **exception work** may keep me useful.
I know other centres may also cut **lead roles**.
I would test **other income** before assuming repair work could support us.
do: Test the **reply queue** and record refund errors from 2026.
Apply for a **paid review post** and trial weekend repairs in the first year.
feel: **Uneasy** about headcount, curious about the tool.
S1.quote: The payroll office counts seats, not pride.
fieldNote: He sees **exception review** as a role to prove with cases.
His **repair trial** uses a familiar family skill rather than a speculative course.
He expects **nearby centres** to face similar software pressures.

steps.text: Test the automated reply queue and log wrong refund answers
Apply for a paid exception-review post when routine chats move
Trial two weekend appliance repairs if his uncle agrees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 means we should ask about paid openings now, not wait for a robot to enter the room. I’d be direct with the manager about how many calls the company expects people to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think cheap thinking AI could do my calls, coaching notes and exception reviews. The robots come around 2031, but a headset job can vanish in 2028. Four months of savings would go quickly if both centres nearby cut staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask for the written staffing forecast and take two paid quality shifts if offered. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for any staffed quality role, while taking weekend repair customers only after my uncle confirms I can do the work safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I still have a few moves. Rosa and I would pause the home search before spending our deposit on a place we could not keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rosa about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Rosa (my partner) that the home search can wait until we know my wage after 2028. We would keep the deposit in cash and pay rent as we do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How real is the repair income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would charge only for repairs I can finish, starting with simple appliance faults beside my uncle. I would not claim two weekends make me a tradesperson.

say: I’d ask for a **staffing forecast** before 2028.
I’d tell colleagues the **thinking-work date** matters first.
I’d ask which **paid openings** remain once AI handles calls.
think: I think AGI could take my **calls and notes**.
I see **2031 robots** as irrelevant to my headset work.
do: Ask for a **written forecast** and paid quality shifts in 2026.
Seek **staffed quality work** and safe weekend repairs after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed**, while seeing a few possible moves.
S2.quote: Four months of savings would go quickly if both centres nearby cut staff.
fieldNote: He correctly anchors his job risk to **2028**, not the robot date.
He would delay a **home purchase** to keep the deposit liquid.
His **repair work** remains limited to safe jobs he can actually do.

steps.text: Pause the home search with Rosa and keep the deposit in cash
Apply for a staffed quality role after 2028
Take simple weekend repairs beside his uncle only after his uncle confirms safe working

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives the centre time to train people honestly, if it intends to keep them. I’d ask for dates and wages attached to any new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years could let me make repairs a genuine second income while I keep my lead wage. But a quality title alone will not beat a system that can reason through every case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d work one Saturday a month with my uncle and track what customers pay after parts. In the first year after 2031, I’d move into a paid quality role if it still exists; otherwise I’d add repair days only if bookings already cover the lost call pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years gives me room to measure the repair work. I’d rather measure repair earnings than tell myself I’m versatile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know repairs could replace wages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count parts, travel and time, not just the cash handed over. If four Saturdays do not cover one lost week of wages, I would not treat repairs as a replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Rosa wants to buy sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Rosa (my partner) wants the home sooner, I’d show her the repair records and the centre’s staffing plan. We can disagree, but I will not spend the deposit on a guess.

say: I’d ask for **dates and wages** on new centre roles.
I’d tell colleagues five years should allow **real training**.
think: I think **repair income** could grow with five years.
I doubt a **quality title** alone protects me from AGI.
do: Work **one Saturday monthly** with my uncle and track net repair pay.
Take **paid quality work** after 2031 if available, adding repairs only with proven bookings.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to test the numbers.
S3.quote: I’d rather measure repair earnings than tell myself I’m versatile.
fieldNote: He measures **net repair pay** after parts and travel.
He keeps the **home deposit** out of uncertain business spending.
He requires **bookings** before replacing call wages with repair days.

steps.text: Work one Saturday monthly with his uncle and record net repair pay
Take a paid quality role after 2031 if one remains
Add repair days after 2031 only if bookings cover lost call wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives young agents time to learn alongside experienced staff before the easy work goes. I’d ask the centre to keep those paid entry shifts open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a decade lets me grow into repair work or another customer role, though I cannot know what a thinking system will leave by 2036. The robots in 2039 could later reach repairs too, so I would not call that a lifetime shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d keep my lead post, save monthly and take a basic appliance safety course paid from my repair income. In the first year after 2036, I’d compare the centre wage with my repair bookings and choose the steadier paid work rather than leave on principle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about my own next few years. A decade lets me test repair earnings before leaving my contact centre wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What course would you actually take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enroll in a local safety course after four paid repair Saturdays cover the fee. Until then I would work beside my uncle and turn down electrical faults I cannot safely handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new agent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still tell a new agent to take a paid first shift if offered. My uncle gave me one, and people need a place to learn where a mistake can be corrected.

say: I’d ask the centre to keep **paid entry shifts** open.
I’d tell new agents to learn beside **experienced staff**.
think: I think ten years gives me **time to build** another income.
I know **2039 robots** could eventually reach repair work too.
do: Keep the **lead job** and save monthly from 2026.
Take a **safety course** once repair earnings cover fees; choose steadier work after comparing wages and bookings in 2036.
feel: **Calm** about the near term, alert to later change.
S4.quote: A decade lets me test repair earnings before leaving my contact centre wage.
fieldNote: He links retraining to **earned repair income**, not borrowed money.
He would choose the **steadier wage** after comparing real bookings.
He values **paid entry shifts** as the route into skilled work.

steps.text: Keep leading the call team through the preparation years
Save a fixed amount monthly from his centre wage
Take an appliance safety course once four paid repair Saturdays cover its fee
Switch to repairs after 2036 only if bookings provide steadier paid work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose both calls and complaint notes before I can prove a new service. I’d need a clear chance to bid for paid quality work and enough notice to turn my side repair work into regular income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who will take an apprentice if the first rung of service work disappears. My uncle taught me repairs by letting me make small mistakes beside him; software cannot give a young worker that first paid shift.

headlineQuote: My uncle taught me repairs by letting me make small mistakes beside him; software cannot give a young worker that first paid shift.
portrait: At **27**, Marco leads customer calls and chats with a two-year diploma and four months of expenses saved.
He earns **typical pay** and has some nearby alternatives, but his job is heavily exposed to thinking AI.
He uses **AI daily**, tests tools early and values work learned beside experienced people.
He would build **repair income** while seeking paid quality work if calls move to AGI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his calls and complaint notes before his side work earns reliably.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid quality role** and early notice would let him prepare his repair work.
